name: Chettikulangara Sree Bhagavathy Temple
tagline: Onattukara’s great Bhagavathy shrine — kettukazhcha, kuthiyottam and temple-prasna guidance
summary: Chettikulangara Sree Bhagavathy Temple at Mavelikkara is a major Bhadrakali shrine in central Kerala, famous for the Kumbha Bharani kettukazhcha and for using Deva/Ashtamangala prasna…
description: Chettikulangara Sree Bhagavathy is a large, centuries‑old Bhadrakali shrine near Mavelikkara in Alappuzha district. The goddess is traditionally honoured in three aspects through the day — as Saraswati in the morning, Lakshmi at noon and Durga/Bhadrakali in the evening.

The temple’s Kumbha Bharani festival (held in Malayalam month Kumbham on the Bharani star) is best known for towering kettukazhcha effigies and the ritual performance Kuthiyottam. The festival and many ritual decisions are fixed by Malayalam-astronomical timing and by specialist temple-astrology (devaprasna/ashtamangala) consultations.

Local communities (13 karas) organise the major offerings and processions; many of the temple’s sub-deities and recent ritual changes were reported to have been placed or revised after devaprashna readings by temple astrologers.

Visitors come for darshan year-round and to witness the festival spectacle in Feb–Mar, but should confirm any ritual‑participation policies beforehand — some practices associated with Kuthiyottam (Chooral/Chooral Muriyal) have attracted legal and rights scrutiny in recent years.
highlights: Kumbha Bharani: kettukazhcha (giant horses, chariots, effigies) and Kuthiyottam.
Temple-astrology (Deva/Ashtamangala prasna) shapes shrine decisions and offerings.
Goddess worshipped in three forms over the course of a day.
Strong community role: 13 karas build the kettukazhcha.
Second-largest temple income under Travancore Devaswom Board (after Sabarimala).

sections.heading: Background
body: Chettikulangara Sree Bhagavathy Temple sits near Mavelikkara and is a major Bhadrakali (Shakta) centre in Onattukara. The shrine has a long local history and is managed under the Travancore Devaswom Board. Records and tradition place the temple among the oldest in the region; the present complex and many ritual structures reflect centuries of local devotion and community contributions.

sections.heading: Prasna and temple‑astrology (how decisions are made)
body: Kerala temples commonly use horary and temple‑specific astrology — Deva Prashna and Ashtamangala Prashna — to ask the deity about wishes, timing, remedies and the need for changes in ritual or shrine layout. In Chettikulangara, recent changes to sub‑deities and some ritual permissions are reported to have followed expert devaprashna readings carried out for the temple.

An Ashtamangala/Deva Prashna combines birth‑chart techniques, special omens, cowrie or shell counting and symbolic procedures (for example the swarna‑arudha or a child placing a coin) to produce detailed recommendations for puja, remedial homams, new prathishtas or festival arrangements. Temple managers and karayogams commonly convene such consultations when long‑standing problems or major festival questions arise.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Darshan: visit at the main puja times and note the temple’s traditional dress code and rules inside the nalambalam. The threefold daily manifestations of the goddess are a distinctive aspect of worship here.

Festival spectacle: Kumbha Bharani (Feb–Mar) is the major event — huge kettukazhcha floats, ritual songs, Kathakali at night and the morning Kuthiyottam performances. During the festival the east paddy fields become the display ground for the community-built effigies.

Observe with respect: the kettukazhcha are community offerings, not theatrical floats, and many rites are vow‑fulfilment acts that have deep local meaning. If you plan to photograph or film rituals, ask permission from the temple or organisers.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Location and timing: the temple is about 4 km west of Mavelikkara and roughly 7 km north of Kayamkulam on SH6. Nearest main railhead is Mavelikkara; the nearest major airport is Kochi (Cochin). Festival dates depend on the Malayalam nakshatra (the Bharani star in Kumbham) — check the current year’s festival announcement before you travel.

Ritual participation and safety: some traditional offerings (notably historic forms of Chooral Muriyal linked to Kuthiyottam) have attracted child‑rights and court attention in past years; confirm current rules and whether special permissions or alternatives are used this season.

latest.text: Kumbha Bharani (Chettikulangara Bharani) was held on 23 February 2026 — the temple’s annual kettukazhcha and Kuthiyottam gatherings draw large crowds; dates are set by the Bharani asterism in Kumbham.

visitorInfo.bestTime: February–March for the Kumbha Bharani festival; October–February for pleasant weather and quieter visits.
visitorInfo.howToReach: By rail: Mavelikkara station (closest). By road: on SH6 (Kayamkulam–Thiruvalla); Chettikulangara is ~4 km west of Mavelikkara. By air: Cochin International Airport (~80–100 km).
etiquette: Respect the temple dress code (traditional attire) and keep footwear outside the nalambalam.
If you intend to attend or observe Kuthiyottam or other vow‑offerings, confirm current permissions and safety provisions with temple management before travel.
Treat kettukazhcha and procession sites as active offerings — avoid standing in construction or pull routes and follow local stewards’ directions.
Ask at the temple office if an Ashtamangala/Deva Prashna has been recently done — the report can explain recent changes in prathishta or ritual timing.
